summary: COP28 in Dubai ended without an explicit agreement to phase out fossil fuels, instead settling on weaker language about "transitioning away" from them and phasing down unabated coal. Fossil fuel lobbyists had unprecedented access and OPEC pressured members to reject fossil-fuel-targeted text. Still, the final text calls for tripling renewable energy capacity by 2030, and clean energy growth is seen as inevitable.
one_line: COP28 came close to a fossil fuel phaseout deal but settled on weaker "transitioning away" language, though it did commit to tripling renewables by 2030.
key_facts: COP28, the 28th UN Conference of the Parties, was held in the United Arab Emirates, a top oil- and gas-producing country, and ran about two weeks.
More than 100 countries pushed for an official agreement to "phase out fossil fuels."
The 2015 Paris accord never mentions coal, oil, or natural gas.

Draft language explicitly calling for a fossil fuel phaseout was removed from the final text; it instead calls for "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner, accelerating action in this critical decade."

The final text calls for "accelerating efforts towards the phase-down of unabated coal power," mirroring language in a letter from COP28 president Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, who is also CEO of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company.

There were more fossil fuel lobbyists at COP28 than at any climate conference in the UN's 28 years of convening it; industry representatives outnumbered every national delegation except the UAE and Brazil.
A BBC and Centre for Climate Reporting investigation found Al Jaber used his COP28 presidency to lobby for oil and gas deals with other governments.
OPEC sent a letter urging member states to "proactively reject any text or formula that targets energy i.e. fossil fuels rather than emissions," after which phaseout language vanished from drafts.
Al Gore said the draft "reads as if OPEC dictated it word for word" and that COP28 was "on the verge of complete failure."
The word "unabated" creates a loophole letting polluters keep burning fossil fuels if paired with carbon capture technologies still unproven at scale.
The final text calls for tripling global renewable energy capacity by 2030, which more than 100 countries had already pledged to do.
The US and China committed to working toward the tripling goal when their climate envoys met in California in November.
The International Energy Agency called the clean energy transition "unstoppable" and forecast that coal, oil, and gas demand would peak this decade.
The world is about 1.2 degrees Celsius hotter on average than before the industrial revolution.
